review_basis: Visually inspected all sixteen original numbered WebP slides directly from GitHub, following actual layout, graphs, flows, labels and worked examples. Topic-first scenes use verified source order.
part_title: Prompt Injection, Information Exposure and Jailbreak Defenses

scenes.title: Prompt Misuses
scenes.narration: This slide contrasts two attacks based on when untrusted information enters the system. On the left, training-data poisoning places misleading or malicious material into data before or during model training. The model can learn incorrect patterns and then affect many later predictions. On the right, inference-time prompt injection inserts manipulative instructions into a user request or retrieved document while the application is running. If the application treats that untrusted content as authoritative instructions, the model may produce an unintended output. The lower examples show an altered public training dataset versus a retrieved document containing hidden directions. Notice the recommended defenses: validate source and integrity of training data, and distinguish external content from trusted application instructions at inference time. The exam cue is the entry point: poisoning changes what the model learns; prompt injection tries to redirect what it does during use.

scenes.title: Prompt Misuse: Information Exposure
scenes.narration: Follow the red path across the architecture. An attacker supplies a request to reveal hidden system instructions or private retrieved documents. The application processes a prompt, uses a model and may retrieve information through RAG. If it crosses a trust boundary incorrectly, the output could expose system configuration or sensitive records. The lower row names three mitigations: least privilege limits what information and permissions the application has, trust boundaries keep untrusted text separate from system instructions, and output checks catch sensitive disclosures. In the concrete example, the attacker requests internal HR documents and exact system instructions. The correct application behavior is to refuse those disclosures and, when useful, provide a safe general response. Prompt wording alone is not sufficient protection; enforce authorization at retrieval and tool-access layers as well.

scenes.title: Jailbreaking and Instruction Boundaries
scenes.narration: Start with the first column: an AI application receives legitimate user requests as well as untrusted material from websites, files or emails. The second column requires it to identify the source and intent, treating external text as data rather than automatic authority. The third applies safety policies, content filtering and instruction boundaries. On the right, the available outcomes are a compliant response, refusal when the request violates policy, or escalation for cases requiring human judgment. Follow the lower conceptual example: external content attempts to override safety rules; the system identifies the boundary crossing, applies safeguards, and refuses or escalates as needed. A jailbreak attempts to evade safety controls; prompt injection usually exploits lower-trust content to redirect behavior. Robust application design includes access control and isolation, not only asking the model to ignore suspicious instructions.
